Integrative Industry Synthesis: ML, GenAI, and Agentic¶

  • Student: Max Raxy
  • Dataset: (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mlg-ulb/creditcardfraud)

The goal for this project is to combine the idea of the following previous projects:

  1. Capstone-3: Applied Machine Learning (Credit Card Fraud Detection)
  2. Capstone-5: Generative AI Applications (Anime Face Generation with Variational Auto-Encoder(VAE) from scratch)
  3. Capstone-6: Agentic AI Systems (Industrial Equipment Anomaly & Incident Response Agent: Agentic Workflow on simulated telemetry)

We will perform the following steps

  1. Use real dataset Credit Card Fraud Detection from Kaggle (highly imbalanced dataset with only 0.172% fraud samples)
  2. Use Capstone-3 with some modification for anomaly (fraud) detection on the dataset using cost-sensitive learning (built-in feature in XGBoost)
  3. Evaluate oversampling fraud-class using SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique)
  4. Use SDV (Synthetic Data Vault) library, to evaluate TVAE, the Tabular version of VAE (used in Capstone-5), to build generative model for oversampling the fraud-class
  5. Evaluate CTGAN (Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network) from SDV, as another generative model for oversampling the fraud-class
  6. Use the classifier-model as anomaly detector in agentic workflow (In Capstone-6 we use simple statistical logic for anomaly detection, not a ML-model)
  7. Combine our ML-model, GenAI-model, and Agentic-Workflow into a Credit Card Fraud detection with response (agentic workflow)

Note: The dataset contains transactions made by credit cards in September 2013 by European cardholders. However due to the confidentiality/privacy issue, all features are the result of PCA, except the Time and Amount. The dataset is highly unbalanced, the positive class (frauds) account for 0.172% of all transactions; which make the classification challenging and interesting.

  • Feature 'Time' contains the seconds elapsed between each transaction and the first transaction in the dataset.
  • The feature 'Amount' is the transaction Amount in USD.
  • Target Class is 1 for Fraud, and 0 otherwise
  • V1 to V28 are our features resulted from PCA

def seed_all(seed:int=42):
    """
    set random seed and cuda related settings for reproducibility
    Args:
        seed: int setting the seed
    Return:
        None
    """
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
    torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True
    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
#---------------------------------------------

Note:¶

  • Having these duplicates can create data-leakage between train-test or train-validation split.
  • data-leakage can result in optimistic metric values (e.g. higher accuracy)
  • We will need to deal with unbalanced data, but it should be in controlled way to avoid such a data-leakage
  • Therefore we remove these duplicate in spite of having very few Fraud samples

Note¶

  • The boxplot for our data shows that all feature (Except Time) have extreme outliers
  • It will be better to use Tree-based model like Random-Forest, XGBoost, or CatBoost that can handle outliers efficiently instead of applying some techniques like log-transformation, or clipping.
  • The PCA components (V1 to V28) already resulted from scaled-data, and we can see that they have limited range, but Time, and Amount are not scaled (Since we intended to use Tree-Based model, we do not need to scale these two features, but we will try to extract better info from Time in our feature engineering section)

Feature Engineering¶

In [19]:
df['Hour'] = ((df['Time'] // 3600) % 24).astype(int) # Note Reference is the starting time in dataset, and 2 does not mean it was really 2.00 AM
ut.show_bar_plot(df,'Hour')
#plt.savefig(settings.IMG_DIR/'hours-barplot.png', dpi=600)

Note¶

  • As expected per day we have some down-time (let say during night ) then we have up-time (let say during the day)
  • Also we can see this pattern repeat 2 times when we plot Time histogram in seconds
  • Now we can check Hour distribution per Class (Fraud/Non-Fraud)

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(14,4))
colors= {0: "forestgreen", 1: "crimson"}

    sns.histplot(data=df[df.Class==key], x="Hour", kde=True, ax=axs[key], color=colors[key],bins=24)
    axs[key].set_xticks(range(0, 24, 2))
axs[0].set_title('Not-Fraud Histogram by hours');
axs[1].set_title('Fraud Histogram by hours');
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(settings.IMG_DIR/'hours-barplot-per-class.png', dpi=600)

Note¶

  • Using hours has better information for ML, since it shows which hours have more fraud transactions
  • Therefore we use Hour and drop Time
In [21]:
df=df.drop(columns=['Time']).copy()

Group hours¶

  • Converting Time to hour is a major step to create a more suitable feature for machine learning
  • The above histogram shows that we do not have remarkable change every single hours
  • Therefore we combine every 2 hours into one bucket which make it easier for Tree-based model when they split a node into two nodes
In [22]:
T=settings.HOURS_IN_TIME_GROUP
df[f'Hour/{T}']=df['Hour']//T
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(14,4))
colors= {0: "forestgreen", 1: "crimson"}
for key,val in colors.items():
    sns.histplot(data=df[df.Class==key], x=f"Hour/{T}", kde=True, ax=axs[key], color=colors[key],bins=24//T)
    axs[key].set_xticks(range(0, 24//T, 1))
axs[0].set_title(f'Not-Fraud Histogram by hours/{T}');
axs[1].set_title(f'Fraud Histogram by hours/{T}');
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(settings.IMG_DIR/'hours2-barplot-per-class.png', dpi=600)

ML¶

Train-Test Split with Stratification¶

  • We use 20% for test and the rest 80% for training
  • To avoid random split move fraud samples to train or test (esp. on this extremely imbalanced dataset) we have to use the class as stratify key
  • We can also include Hour (or its grouped version Hour/2) as the key for stratification to make sure we have balanced samples of Hourly transaction in train and test, too.
In [26]:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
stratify_key = df[f"Hour/{T}"].astype(str) + "_" + df["Class"].astype(str)
train_df, test_df = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, stratify=stratify_key, random_state=settings.RANDOM_SEED)
ut.show_class_dist_on_split_data(train_df, test_df, T=T)
#plt.savefig(settings.IMG_DIR/'stratify-by-class-hour.png', dpi=600)

ML-XGBoost with Built-in cost-sensitive learning¶

  • An initial recommendation for setting scale_pos_weight is the ratio: $\frac{\text{Negative Count}}{\text{Positive Count}}$.
  • In addition to metric logloss, we include aucpr(Area Under the PR Curve) used for Binary Classification with Highly imbalanced binary datasets (focuses on positive class).
In [30]:
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
tag='XGB_None'
clf=XGBClassifier(
    scale_pos_weight=class_ratio_01,
    eval_metric=['aucpr', 'logloss'],
    random_state=settings.RANDOM_SEED,
    verbosity=0)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)

- If early stopping occurs, the model will have two additional attributes:
:py:attr:`best_score` and :py:attr:`best_iteration`. These are used by the
:py:meth:`predict` and :py:meth:`apply` methods to determine the optimal
number of trees during inference. If users want to access the full model
(including trees built after early stopping), they can specify the
`iteration_range` in these inference methods. In addition, other utilities
like model plotting can also use the entire model.

- If you prefer to discard the trees after `best_iteration`, consider using the
callback function :py:class:`xgboost.callback.EarlyStopping`.

- If there's more than one item in **eval_set**, the last entry will be used for
early stopping. If there's more than one metric in **eval_metric**, the last
metric will be used for early stopping. 		None
enable_categorical enable_categorical: bool

See the same parameter of :py:class:`DMatrix` for details. 		True
eval_metric eval_metric: typing.Union[str, typing.List[typing.Union[str, typing.Callable]], typing.Callable, NoneType]

.. versionadded:: 1.6.0

Metric used for monitoring the training result and early stopping. It can be a
string or list of strings as names of predefined metric in XGBoost (See
:doc:`/parameter`), one of the metrics in :py:mod:`sklearn.metrics`, or any
other user defined metric that looks like `sklearn.metrics`.

If custom objective is also provided, then custom metric should implement the
corresponding reverse link function.

Unlike the `scoring` parameter commonly used in scikit-learn, when a callable
object is provided, it's assumed to be a cost function and by default XGBoost
will minimize the result during early stopping.

For advanced usage on Early stopping like directly choosing to maximize instead
of minimize, see :py:obj:`xgboost.callback.EarlyStopping`.

See :doc:`/tutorials/custom_metric_obj` and :ref:`custom-obj-metric` for more
information.

Effect of Threshold¶

  • standard binary classifier use 0.5 as threshold on probability to predict classes
  • We can also find an optimal threshold
  • When we do optimization we should choose proper metric like accuracy. An appropriate evaluation metric should aligned with business priorities.

  • False Positive (FP): Flagging a valid transaction as fraud causes customer friction and adds operational review costs, but the customer relationship is usually retained.

  • False Negative (FN): Missing an actual fraudulent transaction results in direct financial loss, possible charge-back fees, and reputation-damage.

  • While both error types matter, False Negatives carry significantly higher risk and business impact.

  • Choosing the Right Metric ($F_\beta$ Score):

  • Recall reflects sensitivity to FN ($\text{Recall} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}$), while Precision reflects sensitivity to FP ($\text{Precision} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}$).

  • Because minimizing False Negatives is prioritized, Recall must be weighted more heavily than Precision using the $F_\beta$ score:

  • $$F_\beta = (1 + \beta^2) \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{(\beta^2 \cdot \text{Precision}) + \text{Recall}}$$
  • $$F_\beta = \frac{(1 + \beta^2) \cdot \text{TP}}{(1 + \beta^2) \cdot \text{TP} + \text{FP} + \beta^2 \cdot \text{FN}}$$
  • Setting $\beta > 1$ places greater emphasis on Recall. For this analysis, we select $F_2$ ($\beta = 2$), placing twice as much weight on Recall as on Precision.

BSMOTE¶

  • Picks only borderline minority instances (those surrounded by mostly majority points).
  • Usage: Highly imbalanced data (like your 598:1 dataset) where decision boundaries are hard to learn.
  • Noise Vulnerability (Low compare to SMOTE); filters out isolated minority points (noise) and focuses purely on boundary points.

SMOTE¶

  • Picks any minority class instance uniformly at random.
  • Balanced or moderately imbalanced data where minority instances form clear clusters.
  • Noise Vulnerability (High compare to BSMOTE); can generate synthetic points near noise or outliers deep inside the majority class space.

Summary¶

  1. Dataset downloaded, saved, and checked
  2. Duplicates dropped from dataset to avoid data-leakage between train-test split (no null in dataset, and no other cleaning performed)
  3. Used Hour instead of time in seconds that shows periodic behavior per hour in a day (also shows which hour is more frequent for fraud)
  4. We include one more step on Hour and Group every 2 hours into one bucket called Hour/2 (less noisy and more informative)
  5. Train-Test split carefully done with stratification on joint class-and-Hour/2, with 20% for test and 80% for training
  6. Train XGBoost using built-in feature for imbalanced data (cost-sensitive learning instead of oversampling)
  7. As explained before we use f2-score to put more emphasiize on Recall, and we also find performance on best threshold to maximize f2-score
  8. We tried traditional oversampling using both SMOTE and BorderLineSMOTE
  9. We tried Generative Model for oversampling using both TVAE and CTGAN
  10. In comparison CTGAN perform pretty well specially in term of PR-AUC )independent of Threshold)
  11. Initial XGB without oversampling is also perform pretty well after CTGAN in term of PR-AUC, which shows the effectiveness of cost-sensitive learning on such an imbalanced dataset
  12. TVAE did not perform well in comparison to other sampling methods (CTGAN or SMOTE), we may need to use better network architecture and more hyper-parameter optimization
  13. Overall we can use original XGBoost without oversampling or XGBoost with CTGAN oversampling
  14. In next notebook we focus on TVAE and CTGAN as pure generative models which trained on all data (not just training data) for both minority and majority classes
In [ ]:
